claim: HIV-1 integration sites favor active transcription units in the human genome.
source: Although HIV-1 integration sites favor active transcription units in the human genome, high-resolution analysis of individual HIV-1 integration sites has shown that the virus can integrate into a variety of host genomic locations, including non-genic regions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about HIV-1 integration preferences.

claim: HIV-1 can integrate into a variety of host genomic locations, including non-genic regions.
source: Although HIV-1 integration sites favor active transcription units in the human genome, high-resolution analysis of individual HIV-1 integration sites has shown that the virus can integrate into a variety of host genomic locations, including non-genic regions.
evidence: This is supported by high-resolution analysis of HIV-1 integration sites as mentioned in the abstract.

claim: HIV-1 proviruses integrating into non-genic regions are selected for preservation in the host genome during prolonged antiretroviral therapies.
source: The invisible infection by HIV-1 integrating into non-genic regions, challenging the traditional understanding of HIV-1 integration site selection, is more problematic because they are selected for preservation in the host genome during prolonged antiretroviral therapies.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract as a known problem with HIV-1 integration into non-genic regions.

claim: VSV-G-pseudotyped HIV-1 infection initiates the formation of R-loops in both genic and non-genic regions of the host genome.
source: VSV-G-pseudotyped HIV-1 infection initiates the formation of R-loops in both genic and non-genic regions of the host genome and preferentially integrates into R-loop-rich regions.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by DRIPc-seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: HIV-1 preferentially integrates into R-loop-rich regions.
source: VSV-G-pseudotyped HIV-1 infection initiates the formation of R-loops in both genic and non-genic regions of the host genome and preferentially integrates into R-loop-rich regions.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by integration site sequencing data.

claim: Exogenous formation of R-loops directs HIV-1 integration-targeting sites.
source: Using a HeLa cell model that can independently control transcriptional activity and R-loop formation, we demonstrated that the exogenous formation of R-loops directs HIV-1 integration-targeting sites.
evidence: This is demonstrated using the pgR-rich and pgR-poor cell model system as shown in Figure 3.

claim: HIV-1 integrase proteins physically bind to host genomic R-loops.
source: We also found that HIV-1 integrase proteins physically bind to the host genomic R-loops.
evidence: This is supported by EMSA, co-immunoprecipitation, and proximity ligation assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Retroviruses cause permanent host infections by integrating their reverse-transcribed viral genomes into the host genome.
source: Retroviruses cause permanent host infections by integrating their reverse-transcribed viral genomes into the host genome.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Retroviral integration affects the persistence of fatal human diseases and the shaping of metazoan evolution.
source: Retroviral integration considerably affects a wide range of biological phenomena, including the persistence of fatal human diseases and the shaping of metazoan evolution (Johnson, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Johnson, 2019.

claim: The chromosomal landscape of HIV-1 integration influences proviral gene expression, the persistence of integrated proviruses, and prognosis in antiretroviral therapy.
source: The chromosomal landscape of HIV-1 integration has been shown to influence proviral gene expression, the persistence of integrated proviruses, and prognosis in antiretroviral therapy (; Einkauf et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Einkauf et al., 2022 and Jiang et al., 2020.

claim: HIV-1 integration displays distinct preferences for gene-dense regions where active transcription occurs.
source: Integration into the host genome is not random and displays distinct preferences for gene-dense regions, where active transcription occurs (Schröder et al., 2002), by interacting with host factors, such as transcription activators, epigenetic marker binding proteins, and super-enhancers (Achuthan et al., 2018; Ciuffi et al., 2005; Sowd et al., 2016; Lucic et al., 2019; Marini et al., 2015; Kvaratskhelia et al., 2014; Cherepanov et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations including Schröder et al., 2002 and others.

claim: Transcriptional activity is not the sole determinant of the HIV-1 integration site landscape.
source: However, transcriptional activity is not the sole determinant of the HIV-1 integration site landscape (Lucic et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lucic et al., 2019.

claim: Some highly expressed genes do not necessarily correspond to a high level of integration in PBMCs infected in cultures with HIV.
source: For instance, some highly expressed genes do not necessarily correspond to a high level of integration in PBMCs infected in cultures with HIV (Coffin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Coffin et al., 2021.

claim: HIV-1 proviruses are observed in non-genic regions of the genomes of infected individuals.
source: Despite their lower probability of integration, HIV-1 proviruses are observed in non-genic regions of the genomes of infected individuals (Einkauf et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Einkauf et al., 2022.

claim: An R-loop is a three-stranded nucleic acid structure that comprises a DNA-RNA hybrid and a displaced strand of DNA.
source: An R-loop is a three-stranded nucleic acid structure that comprises a DNA-RNA hybrid and a displaced strand of DNA, and has long been considered a transcription byproduct (Niehrs and Luke, 2020; Petermann et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations to Niehrs and Luke, 2020 and Petermann et al., 2022.

claim: R-loops in cellular genomes are enriched in actively transcribed genes.
source: R-loops in cellular genomes are enriched in actively transcribed genes as they occur naturally during transcription (Niehrs and Luke, 2020; Hamperl et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Niehrs and Luke, 2020 and Hamperl et al., 2017.

claim: R-loop formation is not limited to gene body regions and is widespread in the genome.
source: However, R-loop formation is not limited to gene body regions and is widespread in the genome (Niehrs and Luke, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Niehrs and Luke, 2020.

claim: R-loops are abundant in non-genic regions such as intergenic regions and repetitive sequences.
source: As a result of in trans-R-loop formation, R-loops are also abundant in non-genic regions, such as intergenic regions and repetitive sequences, including transposable elements, centromeres, and telomeres (Niehrs and Luke, 2020; Ginno et al., 2012; Lim et al., 2015; Arora et al., 2014), independent of the transcriptional activity of the genes harboring the R-loops.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations including Niehrs and Luke, 2020; Ginno et al., 2012; Lim et al., 2015; Arora et al., 2014.

claim: R-loops relieve superhelical stresses and are often associated with open chromatin marks and active enhancers.
source: In the cellular genome, R-loops relieve superhelical stresses and are often associated with open chromatin marks and active enhancers (Sanz et al., 2016; Chédin, 2016), which are also distributed over HIV-1 integration sites (Schröder et al., 2002; Sowd et al., 2016; Lucic et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sanz et al., 2016 and Chédin, 2016.

claim: A guanine-quadruplex (G4) structure can be generated in the non-template DNA strand of the R-loop during transcription-induced R-loop formation.
source: In transcription-induced R-loop formation, a guanine-quadruplex (G4) structure can be generated in the non-template DNA strand of the R-loop (Lee et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2020.

claim: G4 DNA can influence both productive and latent HIV-1 integration.
source: A recent study showed that G4 DNA can influence both productive and latent HIV-1 integration (Ajoge et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ajoge et al., 2022.

claim: The B-to-A transition in the target DNA occurs during retroviral integration.
source: It has recently been reported that the B-to-A transition in the target DNA occurs during retroviral integration (Jóźwik et al., 2022; Ballandras-Colas et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jóźwik et al., 2022 and Ballandras-Colas et al., 2022.

claim: The number of DRIPc-seq peaks mapped to the human reference genome increased markedly during the early post-infection with HIV-1.
source: Notably, the number of DRIPc-seq peaks mapped to the human reference genome increased markedly during the early post-infection with HIV-1 (3 and 6 hpi for HeLa cells and 6 and 12 hpi for CD4+ and Jurkat T cells; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by DRIPc-seq data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A significant number of unique DRIPc-seq peaks were observed after HIV-1 infection.
source: Most of the peaks that were mapped in cells harvested at 0 hpi were commonly found in all other samples, but a significant number of unique peaks were observed after infection (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by DRIPc-seq data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: R-loop accumulation in HIV-1-infected cells was observed using DNA-RNA hybrid dot blots with anti-S9.6 antibodies.
source: R-loop accumulation in HIV-1-infected cells was observed using DNA-RNA hybrid dot blots with the anti-S9.6 antibodies (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by dot blot data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Dot intensity significantly increased upon HIV-1 infection at 6 hpi.
source: Dot intensity significantly increased upon HIV-1 infection at 6 hpi and the enhanced R-loop signals on the dot blots of HIV-1-infected cells were highly sensitive to in vitro treatment with RNase H (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by dot blot data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The nuclear fluorescence signal associated with R-loops was significantly enhanced in cells infected with HIV-1.
source: After subtracting the nucleolar signal, the nuclear fluorescence signal associated with R-loops was significantly enhanced in cells infected with HIV-1 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Significantly increased R-loop signals that were highly sensitive to RNase H treatment were detected in the P1, P2, and P3 regions of HIV-1-infected cells at 6 hpi.
source: We detected significantly increased R-loop signals that were highly sensitive to RNase H treatment of pre-immunoprecipitates in the P1, P2, and P3 regions of HIV-1-infected cells at 6 hpi compared to those in the cells harvested at 0 hpi (Figure 1—figure supplement 6A).
evidence: This is supported by DRIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6A.

claim: The R-loop signal was enriched even in cells infected with HIV-1 when the reverse transcription or integration of HIV-1 was blocked by enzyme inhibitors.
source: Importantly, the R-loop signal was enriched even in cells infected with HIV-1 when the reverse transcription or integration of HIV-1 was blocked by enzyme inhibitors, such as nevirapine (NVP) or raltegravir (RAL) (Figure 1—figure supplement 6B and C).
evidence: This is supported by dot blot and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6B and C.

claim: Nearly 100% of DRIPc-seq reads from HIV-1-infected HeLa, CD4+, and Jurkat T cells were aligned to the host cellular genome, but not to that of HIV-1.
source: In addition, we confirmed that nearly 100% of DRIPc-seq reads from HIV-1-infected HeLa, CD4+, and Jurkat T cells were aligned to the host cellular genome, but not to that of HIV-1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 6D).
evidence: This is supported by alignment analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6D.

claim: Unique DRIPc-seq peaks observed after HIV-1-infection were numerous and relatively long.
source: Unique DRIPc-seq peaks observed after HIV-1-infection were numerous and relatively long (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by peak length distribution data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A significantly high proportion of DRIPc-seq peaks enrichment upon HIV-1 infection was found in the gene body regions.
source: The presence of R-loops is often correlated with high transcriptional activity, and we found a significantly high proportion of DRIPc-seq peaks enrichment upon HIV-1 infection in the gene body regions (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by genomic feature distribution data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Enrichment of HIV-1-infection-induced DRIPc-seq peaks proportions was observed in intergenic or repeat regions.
source: However, we also observed enrichment of HIV-1-infection-induced DRIPc-seq peaks proportions mapped to intergenic or repeat regions, including short interspersed nuclear elements (SINEs), long interspersed nuclear elements (LINEs), and long terminal repeat (LTR) retrotransposons, where transcription is typically repressed (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by genomic feature distribution data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The proportion of DRIPc-seq peaks mapped to various genomic compartments remained consistent over the hours following HIV-1 infection.
source: In addition, the proportion of DRIPc-seq peaks mapped to various genomic compartments remained consistent over the hours following HIV-1 infection (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by temporal analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The expression levels of SINEs, LINEs, and LTRs were lower at both 3 and 6 hpi compared with those at 0 hpi.
source: In contrast, we found that the expression levels of SINEs, LINEs, and LTRs were even lower at both 3 and 6 hpi compared with those at 0 hpi whereas HIV-1-induced R-loops were significantly accumulated compared with those at 0 hpi (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The expression profile of genes harboring HIV-1-induced R-loops in their gene bodies showed very weak correlations with the signals of DRIPc-seq peaks at 3 hpi and at 6 hpi.
source: The expression profile of genes harboring HIV-1-induced R-loops in their gene bodies showed very weak correlations with the signals of DRIPc-seq peaks at 3 hpi (Pearson's r=0.21, p=1.08 × 10–84; Figure 2D) and at 6 hpi (Pearson's r=–0.34, p=2.40 × 10–228; Figure 2D), which implies that the unique R-loop peaks upon HIV-1 infection do not engage in a transcriptional burst.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: pgR-rich cells showed significantly higher luciferase activity only when R-loops were induced by DOX treatment.
source: Notably, we found that pgR-rich cells showed significantly higher luciferase activity only when R-loops were induced by DOX treatment, whereas pgR-poor cells showed comparable luciferase activity regardless of transcriptional activation by DOX treatment (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Integration events were significantly higher in pgR-rich cells only when R-loops were induced by DOX treatment.
source: Remarkably, integration events were significantly higher in pgR-rich cells only when R-loops were induced by DOX treatment (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by integration site sequencing data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The number of HIV-1 integration-seq mapped reads within the non-R-loop forming sequence in pgR-poor cells remained very low, even after transcriptional activation by DOX treatment.
source: However, the number of HIV-1 integration-seq mapped reads within the non-R-loop forming sequence in pgR-poor cells remained very low, even after transcriptional activation by DOX treatment (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by integration site sequencing data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: HIV-1 integration was enriched in the vicinity of R-loop forming regions in the pgR-rich cell line upon DOX treatment.
source: HIV-1 integration was enriched in the vicinity of R-loop forming regions in the pgR-rich cell line upon DOX treatment, but the enrichment was not observed in pgR-poor cells that did not form stable R-loops, even after transcriptional activation by DOX treatment (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This is supported by heat map data shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: Approximately three to four times more integration was detected in the R-loop regions than in other genomic regions without R-loops in HeLa cells, CD4+, and Jurkat T cells.
source: Notably, we detected approximately three to four times more integration in the R-loop regions than in other genomic regions without R-loops in HeLa cells, CD4+, and Jurkat T cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by integration site quantification data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: HIV-1 integration sites preferred the central and nearby areas of the R-loops regions.
source: Notably, HIV-1 integration sites preferred the centeral and nearby areas of the R-loops regions (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by distance distribution analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Biases in HIV-1 integration were observed in HIV-1-induced R-loop-positive regions, P1-P3.
source: We observed biases in HIV-1 integration in HIV-1-induced R-loop-positive regions, P1-P3, which showed highly induced R-loop signals upon HIV-1 infection in DRIPc-seq analysis and DRIP-qPCR (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by genome browser data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: HIV-1 integration sites were not detected in the R-loop-negative regions N1 and N2.
source: In contrast, HIV-1 integration sites were not detected in the R-loop-negative regions N1 and N2 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by genome browser data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The nucleic acid substrate consisting of an R-loop structure bound to HIV-1 integrase proteins with higher binding affinity than that of the simple dsDNA duplex.
source: Notably, the nucleic acid substrate consisted of an R-loop structure bound to HIV-1 integrase proteins with higher binding affinity than that of the simple dsDNA duplex (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: R-loop composing forms of nucleic acid structures, such as RNA-DNA hybrid with exposed ssDNA (R:D+ssDNA) and RNA-DNA hybrid (hybrid), showed high binding affinity to integrases.
source: Additionally, the R-loop composing forms of nucleic acid structures, such as RNA-DNA hybrid with exposed ssDNA (R:D+ssDNA) and RNA-DNA hybrid (hybrid), also showed high binding affinity to integrases (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and Figure 5A.

claim: HIV-1 integrase proteins co-immunoprecipitated with R-loops.
source: Under our experimental conditions, R-loops were reproducibly immunoprecipitated (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) and HIV-1 integrase proteins co-immunoprecipitated with the R-loops (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: DNA-RNA hybrids co-immunoprecipitated with the positive control H3 but not with the negative controls LaminA/C and Actin.
source: DNA-RNA hybrids also co-immunoprecipitated with the positive control H3 (Cristini et al., 2018) but not with the negative controls LaminA/C and Actin (Cristini et al., 2018; Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5C and citations to Cristini et al., 2018.

claim: The S9.6 signal of the immunoprecipitated nucleic acids was highly sensitive to RNase H treatment of the pre-immunoprecipitates.
source: The S9.6 signal of the immunoprecipitated nucleic acids were highly sensitive to RNase H treatment of the pre-immunoprecipitates (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by dot blot data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The blotting signal of the co-immunoprecipitated HIV-1 integrase and H3 proteins was significantly reduced upon RNase H treatment.
source: Accordingly, the blotting signal of the co-immunoprecipitated HIV-1 integrase and H3 proteins was significantly reduced upon RNase H treatment (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: R-loops were immunoprecipitated using HIV-1 integrase, and the S9.6 signal of immunoprecipitated nucleic acids was highly sensitive to RNase H treatment.
source: We performed reciprocal immunoprecipitation using an anti-FLAG monoclonal antibody and detected the immunoprecipitated R-loops using dot blot analysis with anti-S9.6. R-loops, which were immunoprecipitated using HIV-1 integrase, and the S9.6 signal of immunoprecipitated nucleic acids was highly sensitive to RNase H treatment (Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by dot blot data shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: PLA signals significantly increased upon HIV-1 infection.
source: PLA signals in non-infected cells were comparable to those in S9.6-alone and GFP-alone single antibody-negative controls; however, PLA signals significantly increased upon HIV-1 infection (Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by PLA data shown in Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: R-loops display enhancer and insulator chromatin states that can act as distal regulatory elements by recruiting diverse chromatin binding factors.
source: The R-loops display enhancer and insulator chromatin states, that can act as distal regulatory elements by recruiting diverse chromatin binding factors (Sanz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sanz et al., 2016.

claim: LEDGF/p75 and CPSF6 are two decisive host factors that direct HIV-1 integration by interacting with integrase or trafficking the viral preintegration complex towards the nuclear interior.
source: LEDGF/p75 (Sowd et al., 2016; Cherepanov et al., 2003; Schrijvers et al., 2012) and CPSF6 (Achuthan et al., 2018; Sowd et al., 2016) are two decisive host factors that direct HIV-1 integration by interacting with integrase or trafficking the viral preintegration complex towards the nuclear interior (Achuthan et al., 2018; Sowd et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations including Sowd et al., 2016; Cherepanov et al., 2003; Schrijvers et al., 2012; Achuthan et al., 2018.

claim: LEDGF/p75 and CPSF6 have been identified as potential R-loop-binding proteins in DNA-RNA interactome analysis and R-loop proximity proteomics.
source: In fact, these host factors have recently been identified as potential R-loop-binding proteins in DNA-RNA interactome analysis (Cristini et al., 2018) and R-loop proximity proteomics (Mosler et al., 2021), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cristini et al., 2018 and Mosler et al., 2021.

claim: The Fanconi anemia pathway is a well-known R-loop regulatory pathway.
source: For example, the Fanconi anemia pathway (García-Rubio et al., 2015; Giannini et al., 2020), a well-known R-loop regulatory pathway, has been recently proposed as an HIV-1 integration regulatory factor exploited by HIV-1 (Fu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to García-Rubio et al., 2015 and Giannini et al., 2020.

claim: The Fanconi anemia pathway has been recently proposed as an HIV-1 integration regulatory factor exploited by HIV-1.
source: For example, the Fanconi anemia pathway (García-Rubio et al., 2015; Giannini et al., 2020), a well-known R-loop regulatory pathway, has been recently proposed as an HIV-1 integration regulatory factor exploited by HIV-1 (Fu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fu et al., 2022.

claim: During retroviral integration, the target DNA undergoes a transition of its conformation from B-form to A-form.
source: Recent advancements in cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) technology have revealed the conformational characteristics of the target DNA during retroviral integration (Jóźwik et al., 2022; Ballandras-Colas et al., 2022). During retroviral integration, the target DNA undergoes a transition of its conformation from B-form to A-form.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jóźwik et al., 2022 and Ballandras-Colas et al., 2022.

claim: R-loops represent intermediates between the B-form DNA and A-form RNA conformations.
source: R-loops, which represent intermediates between the B-form DNA and A-form RNA conformations (Jóźwik et al., 2022), may have an intrinsic preferential binding ability to retroviral intasomes over other nucleic acid structures.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jóźwik et al., 2022.

claim: The HIV-1 accessory protein Vpr causes genomic damage.
source: For instance, the HIV-1 accessory protein Vpr causes genomic damage (Li et al., 2020a) and transcriptomic changes during the early stages post-infection (Bauby et al., 2021), both of which can lead to in cis and in trans-R-loop formation (Petermann et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2020a.

claim: The HIV-1 accessory protein Vpr causes transcriptomic changes during the early stages post-infection.
source: For instance, the HIV-1 accessory protein Vpr causes genomic damage (Li et al., 2020a) and transcriptomic changes during the early stages post-infection (Bauby et al., 2021), both of which can lead to in cis and in trans-R-loop formation (Petermann et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bauby et al., 2021.

claim: APOBEC3 regulates cellular R-loop levels.
source: Another HIV-1 accessory protein, Vif, counteracts the host antiviral factor, APOBEC3 (Stopak et al., 2003; Kmiec and Kirchhoff, 2024), which was recently found to regulates cellular R-loop levels (McCann et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to McCann et al., 2021.

claim: HIV-1 proviruses are found in non-genic regions.
source: Although most HIV-1 integration occurs in genic regions (Einkauf et al., 2022; Schröder et al., 2002), HIV-1 proviruses are also found in non-genic regions (Yukl et al., 2018), and understanding these 'transcriptionally silent' proviruses is critical for developing strategies to completely eliminate HIV-1.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yukl et al., 2018.

claim: In HIV-1 elite controllers, HIV-1 proviruses in heterochromatic regions are not eliminated but selected by the immune system.
source: In HIV-1 elite controllers, who suppress viral gene expression to undetectable levels, HIV-1 proviruses in heterochromatic regions are not eliminated but selected by the immune system (Jiang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jiang et al., 2020.

claim: Proviruses with lower expression levels can persist in the host genome even during antiretroviral therapy.
source: Moreover, proviruses with lower expression levels can persist in the host genome even during antiretroviral therapy (Einkauf et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Einkauf et al., 2022.

claim: R-loops may represent the mechanism by which HIV-1 achieves 'invisible' and permanent infection in non-genic regions.
source: We propose that R-loops, particularly those enriched in non-genic regions, may represent the mechanism by which the virus achieves 'invisible' and permanent infection.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the findings of the study.

claim: Transcriptional activity itself is not sufficient for HIV-1 integration site determination.
source: The results indicated that host genomic R-loops are preferred by HIV-1 integration. Moreover, our data suggest that transcriptional activity itself is not sufficient for HIV-1 integration site determination, but that the formation of R-loops accounts for HIV-1 integration site selection.
evidence: This is inferred from the pgR-rich and pgR-poor cell model experiments.

claim: The formation of R-loops accounts for HIV-1 integration site selection.
source: The results indicated that host genomic R-loops are preferred by HIV-1 integration. Moreover, our data suggest that transcriptional activity itself is not sufficient for HIV-1 integration site determination, but that the formation of R-loops accounts for HIV-1 integration site selection.
evidence: This is inferred from the pgR-rich and pgR-poor cell model experiments.

claim: R-loops are important components of the host genomic environment for HIV-1 integration site determination.
source: Our results suggest that R-loops are important components of the host genomic environment for HIV-1 integration site determination.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results in the study.

claim: Host cellular R-loop accumulation upon HIV-1 infection is widely distributed in both genic and non-genic regions and is not necessarily correlated with the expression levels of the genes harboring the R-loops.
source: Together, our data demonstrate that host cellular R-loop accumulation upon HIV-1 infection is widely distributed in both genic and non-genic regions and is not necessarily correlated with the expression levels of the genes harboring the R-loops.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from DRIPc-seq and RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: HIV-1 infection induces host cellular R-loop enrichment at early post-infection.
source: Together, these data demonstrated that HIV-1 infection induces host genomic R-loop enrichment at early post-infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple biochemical and sequencing experiments.

claim: HIV-1 infection regulates R-loop dynamics in host cells, possibly by inducing either new R-loop formation or stabilizing existing R-loops in the host cellular genome.
source: This also suggests that HIV-1 infection regulates R-loop dynamics in host cells, possibly by inducing either new R-loop formation or stabilizing existing R-loops in the host cellular genome.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed R-loop accumulation.

claim: The enrichment of R-loop signals in cells originates from the host genome, but not from DNA-RNA hybrid formation during the viral life cycle or transcriptional burst from integrated HIV-1 proviruses.
source: This result indicates that the enrichment of R-loop signals in cells originates from the host genome, but not from DNA-RNA hybrid formation during the viral life cycle or transcriptional burst from integrated HIV-1 proviruses.
evidence: This is inferred from experiments using reverse transcription and integration inhibitors.

claim: R-loops induced by HIV-1 infection occupy a genomic region larger than that of the R-loops without HIV-1 infection.
source: Unique DRIPc-seq peaks observed after HIV-1-infection were numerous and relatively long (Figure 2A). This suggests that the R-loops induced by HIV-1 infection occupy a genomic region larger than that of the R-loops without HIV-1 infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the peak length distribution data.

claim: HIV-1 infection does not induce R-loop enrichment at specific genomic features, but R-loop accumulation after HIV-1 infection is widely distributed.
source: This suggests that HIV-1 infection does not induce R-loop enrichment at specific genomic features, but that R-loop accumulation after HIV-1 infection is widely distributed.
evidence: This is inferred from the consistent proportion of DRIPc-seq peaks across genomic compartments over time.

claim: The unique R-loop peaks upon HIV-1 infection do not engage in a transcriptional burst.
source: The expression profile of genes harboring HIV-1-induced R-loops in their gene bodies showed very weak correlations with the signals of DRIPc-seq peaks at 3 hpi (Pearson's r=0.21, p=1.08 × 10–84; Figure 2D) and at 6 hpi (Pearson's r=–0.34, p=2.40 × 10–228; Figure 2D), which implies that the unique R-loop peaks upon HIV-1 infection do not engage in a transcriptional burst.
evidence: This is inferred from the weak correlation between R-loop signals and gene expression.

claim: R-loops are an important component of the host genomic environment for HIV-1 integration site determination.
source: Overall, our results from bioinformatics analysis using different types of naïve host cells infected with HIV-1 are consistent with the idea that the virus has a preference for targeting R-loop-forming regions for integration (Figure 3), suggesting that R-loops are an important component of the host genomic environment for HIV-1 integration site determination.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from integration site analysis across multiple cell types.

claim: R-loops may have an intrinsic preferential binding ability to retroviral intasomes over other nucleic acid structures.
source: R-loops, which represent intermediates between the B-form DNA and A-form RNA conformations (Jóźwik et al., 2022), may have an intrinsic preferential binding ability to retroviral intasomes over other nucleic acid structures.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on structural considerations.

claim: R-loops are another putative host factor driving HIV-1 integration site determination.
source: Considering theses previous studies and our current findings, we propose R-loops as another putative host factor driving HIV-1 integration site determination, and a possible intermediate regulator of HIV-1 integration site selection by such host proteins.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the study's findings and previous literature.

claim: R-loops may be a possible intermediate regulator of HIV-1 integration site selection by host proteins.
source: Considering theses previous studies and our current findings, we propose R-loops as another putative host factor driving HIV-1 integration site determination, and a possible intermediate regulator of HIV-1 integration site selection by such host proteins.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the study's findings and previous literature.

claim: R-loop regions exhibit increased chromatin accessibility.
source: R-loop regions exhibit increased chromatin accessibility.
evidence: This is stated as a known property of R-loops in the discussion.

claim: R-loops may drive R-loop-mediated integration over long-range genomic regions.
source: This not only allows R-loops to drive dynamics in the genome, but also possibly drives R-loop-mediated integration over long-range genomic regions.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of how R-loops might influence integration.

claim: Virion-associated HIV-1 proteins may be responsible for inducing R-loops.
source: Our study showed the host genomic R-loops significantly accumulate shortly after HIV-1 infection. Thus, it is possible that virion-associated HIV-1 proteins are responsible for inducing these R-loops.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the mechanism behind R-loop induction.

claim: Genomic damage and transcriptomic changes can lead to in cis and in trans-R-loop formation.
source: For instance, the HIV-1 accessory protein Vpr causes genomic damage (Li et al., 2020a) and transcriptomic changes during the early stages post-infection (Bauby et al., 2021), both of which can lead to in cis and in trans-R-loop formation (Petermann et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Petermann et al., 2022.

claim: Vif counteracts the host antiviral factor APOBEC3.
source: Another HIV-1 accessory protein, Vif, counteracts the host antiviral factor, APOBEC3 (Stopak et al., 2003; Kmiec and Kirchhoff, 2024), which was recently found to regulates cellular R-loop levels (McCann et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Stopak et al., 2003 and Kmiec and Kirchhoff, 2024.

claim: Most HIV-1 integration occurs in genic regions.
source: Although most HIV-1 integration occurs in genic regions (Einkauf et al., 2022; Schröder et al., 2002), HIV-1 proviruses are also found in non-genic regions (Yukl et al., 2018), and understanding these 'transcriptionally silent' proviruses is critical for developing strategies to completely eliminate HIV-1.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Einkauf et al., 2022 and Schröder et al., 2002.

claim: Understanding 'transcriptionally silent' proviruses is critical for developing strategies to completely eliminate HIV-1.
source: Although most HIV-1 integration occurs in genic regions (Einkauf et al., 2022; Schröder et al., 2002), HIV-1 proviruses are also found in non-genic regions (Yukl et al., 2018), and understanding these 'transcriptionally silent' proviruses is critical for developing strategies to completely eliminate HIV-1.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for studying HIV-1 integration in non-genic regions.

claim: HIV-1 elite controllers suppress viral gene expression to undetectable levels.
source: In HIV-1 elite controllers, who suppress viral gene expression to undetectable levels, HIV-1 proviruses in heterochromatic regions are not eliminated but selected by the immune system (Jiang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of HIV-1 elite controllers.

claim: The mechanism by which HIV-1 targets gene-silent regions for 'invisible' integration remains unclear.
source: However, the mechanism by which HIV-1 targets gene-silent regions for 'invisible' integration remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: R-loops are enriched in both genic and non-genic regions during HIV-1 infection.
source: Our study has revealed that R-loops are enriched in both genic and non-genic regions during HIV-1 infection, and that the virus preferentially targets these R-loops for integration.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: HIV-1 preferentially targets R-loops for integration.
source: Our study has revealed that R-loops are enriched in both genic and non-genic regions during HIV-1 infection, and that the virus preferentially targets these R-loops for integration.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: HIV-1 exploits and frequently targets the host genomic R-loop regions for successful integration and infection.
source: These results demonstrate that HIV-1 exploits and frequently targets the host genomic R-loop regions for successful integration and infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: R-loops may play a collaborative role with host factors governing the HIV-1 integration site selection.
source: Another possible explanation for the preference of HIV-1 integration for host genomic R-loops is that R-loops may play a collaborative role with host factors governing the HIV-1 integration site selection.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of how R-loops might influence integration.

claim: Cellular R-loops are recognized and regulated by numerous cellular proteins.
source: Cellular R-loops are recognized and regulated by numerous cellular proteins (Cristini et al., 2018; Mosler et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cristini et al., 2018 and Mosler et al., 2021.

claim: R-loops are tightly regulated by DNA damage response proteins.
source: R-loops are tightly regulated by DNA damage response proteins (Stirling and Hieter, 2017) and the DNA repair machinery plays an important role in the HIV-1 integration process (Lesbats et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Stirling and Hieter, 2017 and Lesbats et al., 2016.

claim: The DNA repair machinery plays an important role in the HIV-1 integration process.
source: R-loops are tightly regulated by DNA damage response proteins (Stirling and Hieter, 2017) and the DNA repair machinery plays an important role in the HIV-1 integration process (Lesbats et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lesbats et al., 2016.

claim: The R-loop structure may drive dynamics in the genomic environment and the spatial organization of the genome, resulting in increased accessibility of HIV-1 intasome binding to the target host genomic region.
source: One possible explanation for why HIV-1 integration shows a preference for host genomic R-loop regions is that the R-loop structure may drive dynamics in the genomic environment and the spatial organization of the genome, resulting in increased accessibility of HIV-1 intasome binding to the target host genomic region.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the mechanism behind R-loop preference.
